sections.title: Physics of the Eye
objectives: Explain the image formation by the eye.
Explain why peripheral images lack detail and color.
Analyze the accommodation of the eye for distant and near vision.

misconceptions.claim: The eye focuses by moving its lens.
misconceptions.correction: It focuses by changing the shape of its lens, which is what the ciliary muscles do.

summary: Image formation by the eye is adequately described by the thin lens equations: P=1do+1di and hiho=−dido=m.
The eye produces a real image on the retina by adjusting its focal length and power in a process called accommodation.
For close vision, the eye is fully accommodated and has its greatest power, whereas for distant vision, it is totally relaxed and has its smallest power.

sections.title: Vision Correction
objectives: Identify and discuss common vision defects.

misconceptions.claim: A short-sighted person is given a converging lens to correct their sight.
misconceptions.correction: They are given a diverging lens. A short-sighted eye focuses distant light in front of the retina, and a diverging lens spreads the rays so that the focus moves back onto the retina. A converging lens corrects long sight, not short sight.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-3, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the diverging lens as the answer.

summary: Nearsightedness, or myopia, is the inability to see distant objects and is corrected with a diverging lens to reduce power.
Farsightedness, or hyperopia, is the inability to see close objects and is corrected with a converging lens to increase power.
In myopia and hyperopia, the corrective lenses produce images at a distance that the person can see clearly—the far point and near point, respectively.

sections.title: Color and Color Vision
objectives: Explain the simple theory of color vision.
Outline the coloring properties of light sources.
Describe the retinex theory of color vision.

misconceptions.claim: The colour of an object is a fixed property of the object, whatever light falls on it.
misconceptions.correction: The colour seen depends on both the object and the light source. A red object looks black under green light because it reflects very little green.

misconceptions.claim: The primary colours of light are red, yellow and blue, the same as for paints.
misconceptions.correction: The primary colours of light are red, green and blue. Mixing all three adds to white. Pigments subtract colours, so their primaries are different.

summary: The eye has four types of light receptors—rods and three types of color-sensitive cones.
The rods are good for night vision, peripheral vision, and motion changes, while the cones are responsible for central vision and color.
We perceive many hues, from light having mixtures of wavelengths.

authored_exercises.stem: What are the three primary colours of light?
solution: Additive colour mixing uses red, green and blue light.
Red and green together make yellow.
All three together make white.

authored_exercises.stem: Why does a white sheet look white in sunlight?
authored_exercises.answer: It reflects all visible wavelengths strongly and about equally.
solution: Sunlight contains all visible colours.
A white surface reflects them all without strongly absorbing any one.
The reflected light reaching the eye is therefore a mixture that looks white.

authored_exercises.stem: A blue object is illuminated with yellow light. What colour does it appear, and why?
authored_exercises.answer: It appears black, because the blue object reflects mainly blue light and yellow light contains no blue to reflect.
solution: The object’s pigment absorbs most wavelengths except blue.
Yellow light is a mixture of red and green wavelengths.
With no blue present to reflect, the object reflects very little light and looks black.

sections.no_worked_example_reason: The source section on Color and Color Vision has no worked example; the teaching text derives the key results and the practice set applies them.

sections.title: Microscopes
objectives: Learn how image is formed in a compound microscope.

misconceptions.claim: A magnifying glass works by making the object bigger.
misconceptions.correction: It works by making the object subtend a larger angle at the eye, not by changing the object.

misconceptions.claim: The magnifying power of a compound microscope is increased by using an eyepiece of longer focal length.
misconceptions.correction: A shorter eyepiece focal length gives a larger angular magnification, because the eyepiece acts as a simple magnifier. A shorter objective focal length also increases the magnification.
misconceptions.locator: candidate trap trap-4, demoted pending paper evidence
misconceptions.signal: Our own question offers the longer eyepiece as an option.

summary: The microscope is a multiple-element system having more than a single lens or mirror.

Many optical devices contain more than a single lens or mirror. These are analysed by considering each element sequentially. The image formed by the first is the object for the second, and so on. The same ray tracing and thin lens techniques apply to each lens element.

The overall magnification of a multiple-element system is the product of the magnifications of its individual elements. For a two-element system with an objective and an eyepiece, this is m=mome, where mo is the magnification of the objective and me is the magnification of the eyepiece, such as for a microscope.

sections.title: Telescopes
objectives: Outline the invention of a telescope.
Describe the working of a telescope.

misconceptions.claim: A telescope makes a distant object larger by physically enlarging it.
misconceptions.correction: A telescope collects more light and makes the object subtend a larger angle at the eye. The object itself is unchanged.

misconceptions.claim: The eyepiece of a telescope is the large lens at the front.
misconceptions.correction: The large front lens is the objective. It gathers light and forms a real image; the eyepiece magnifies that image.

summary: Simple telescopes can be made with two lenses. They are used for viewing objects at large distances and utilize the entire range of the electromagnetic spectrum.

The angular magnification M for a telescope is given by M=θ′θ=−fofe, where θ is the angle subtended by an object viewed by the unaided eye, θ′ is the angle subtended by a magnified image, and fo and fe are the focal lengths of the objective and the eyepiece.

sections.title: Aberrations
objectives: Distinguish spherical aberration from chromatic aberration.
Explain how compound lenses and stops reduce aberrations.

misconceptions.claim: Chromatic aberration can be removed by stopping down the aperture.
misconceptions.correction: Stopping down the aperture reduces spherical aberration and improves sharpness, but it does not remove chromatic aberration. Chromatic aberration is corrected with a compound lens made of two glasses.

summary: Aberrations or image distortions can arise due to the finite thickness of optical instruments, imperfections in the optical components, and limitations on the ways in which the components are used.
The means for correcting aberrations range from better components to computational techniques.

authored_exercises.answer: A defect in which rays far from the axis of a spherical lens or mirror are focused at a different point from rays near the axis.
solution: A spherical surface does not focus all parallel rays to one point.
Rays near the edge come to a focus closer to the lens than paraxial rays.
The result is a blurred image.

authored_exercises.stem: A telescope has an objective of focal length 80 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 4 cm. Find its angular magnification.
solution: For a telescope in normal adjustment, angular magnification M = f_o/f_e.

authored_exercises.stem: A compound microscope has an objective of focal length 1.0 cm and an eyepiece of focal length 5.0 cm. The tube length is 15 cm. Estimate the angular magnification.
solution: Use M ≈ (L/f_o)(25 cm/f_e).

(b) What is this image’s magnification? (c) An eyepiece with a 2.00 cm focal length is placed 20.0 cm from the objective. Where is the final image? (d) What magnification is produced by the eyepiece? (e) What is the overall magnification?

solution: (b) With the 100× objective: $M_{total}=100×4.00=400$. With the 400× objective: $M_{total}=400×4.00=1600$.
